# Supplement {#sec-supplement}

This supplement reports every measure of @sec-measures for each experiment: the
baseline in full (@sec-supp-baseline), then the null-space and roll-up experiments
(@sec-supp-null, @sec-supp-rollup), whose effects are summarized in
@sec-supp-remedies. Within an experiment, every table pools the cells or the draws
of the four PUMAs, each panel is one value of $\alpha$, and the long HMC run of the
same experiment and $\alpha$ is the reference posterior. IPF and IPF with
multinomial draws have no $\alpha$, so they are shown once, in their own panel,
except in the agreement tables, where they are compared with each $\alpha$'s
reference. IPF is raked to the block group margins of the six tables published at
block group level and to the tract margins of the three tables published only at
tract level (B17024, B23001 and B26001).

## Baseline {#sec-supp-baseline}

### Fit to the published constraints {#sec-supp-fit}

::: {#tbl-fit-bg}

```{=latex}
\input{results/table2_baseline.tex}
```

Baseline: fit to the published block group constraints. Block group constraint leaf
cells of the four PUMAs pooled, sampled cells only (nonzero estimates with a
sampling variance). Coverage: the share of cells whose published estimate lies
between the 5th and 95th percentiles of the method's draws. $|z|$ p90: the 90th
percentile over cells of $|\bar m - \hat y|/\mathrm{SE}$. Half-width / MOE: the
half-width of the 90 percent interval over the published margin of error, median
over cells. Interval score / SE: as in @sec-measures-published, mean over cells.

:::

::: {#tbl-fit-tract}

```{=latex}
\input{results/table2t_baseline.tex}
```

Baseline: fit to the published tract constraints. As @tbl-fit-bg, for tract cells.

:::

@tbl-fit-bg compares each method's draws with the published block group estimates
used as constraints. Because these estimates were used in fitting, coverage has no
nominal level; it describes the fit rather than calibration. A half-width below the
published margin of error is not in itself a defect, since the posterior combines
each estimate with the other constraints and the survey records and may
legitimately be more precise than the estimate alone; a half-width near zero is.

The Laplace approximation stands apart. Its intervals are a negligible fraction of
the published margins of error (median ratio 0.00 at $\alpha = 0.01$ and 0.12 at
$\alpha = 1$), they contain the published estimate in only 5 and 17 percent of
cells, and the 90th percentile of $|z|$ exceeds 11. The Laplace draws express
near-certainty about counts that the ACS publishes with substantial error. The
variational and HMC draws, by contrast, have intervals comparable to the published
margins of error (median ratios 0.93 to 1.13), contain the published value in 95
to 99 percent of cells, and lie within about one standard error of it in 90 percent
of cells. IPF reproduces the block group estimates almost exactly ($|z|$ p90 of
0.06 [UPDATE]); since those estimates are noisy, this is better understood as
fitting their sampling error than as accuracy, and its multinomial replicates vary
by about a quarter of the published margin of error [UPDATE]. The tract constraints
(@tbl-fit-tract) show the same pattern for the posterior methods; IPF's tract
$|z|$ p90 is [UPDATE] now that it is also raked to the tract-only tables.

### Accuracy on tables not used as constraints {#sec-supp-heldout}

::: {.landscape}

::: {#tbl-heldout}

```{=latex}
\input{results/table3_baseline.tex}
```

Baseline: accuracy on held-out ACS tables at block group level; leaf cells of the
four PUMAs pooled, sampled cells only. Coverage and $|z|$ p90 as in @tbl-fit-bg. The interval
is for the true count, while the published value also carries sampling error, so
coverage below 0.90 is expected even for a correct model. Interval score / SE: the
width of a 90 percent predictive interval for the published value plus 20 times
how far the published value falls outside it, in published SEs, mean over cells
[@gneiting2007strictly]; a method that knew every true count would score about
4.13.

:::

:::

::: {#tbl-heldout-tract}

```{=latex}
\input{results/table3t_baseline.tex}
```

Baseline: accuracy on held-out tables at tract level. As @tbl-heldout, for tract
cells.

:::

@tbl-heldout reports accuracy on published block group tables withheld from the
fit (e.g., [EXAMPLE]), pooled over all held-out tables.

Two results stand out. First, $\alpha = 0.01$ is consistently more accurate than
$\alpha = 1$: under the reference posterior, coverage is [UPDATE] against [UPDATE]
and $|z|$ p90 is [UPDATE] against [UPDATE]. One possible explanation is that
the correlations among the constraint estimates carry information about structure
shared with the held-out tables; another is that the diagonal covariance at
$\alpha = 1$ counts nested totals several times, and so fits the constraints, and
their sampling errors, too closely. We have not distinguished between these.
Second, the posterior mean is not uniformly more accurate than IPF's single
solution: IPF's $|z|$ p90 ([UPDATE]) is to be compared with those of the
$\alpha = 0.01$ posteriors ([UPDATE]) and the $\alpha = 1$ posteriors
([UPDATE]). What IPF lacks is a usable statement of uncertainty: its
multinomial replicates contain the published value in [UPDATE] of the cells. The
Laplace approximation is again far from the published values ($|z|$ p90 above 10).

These comparisons are probably optimistic. The held-out and constraint estimates
come from the same ACS sample, so their sampling errors are correlated, and fitting
the constraints partly fits the errors of the held-out estimates too. Consistent
with this, the 90th percentile of $|z|$ for the best methods (1.21) is below the
1.645 that would be expected even of the true counts.

### Agreement with the reference posterior {#sec-supp-agree}

::: {#tbl-agree}

```{=latex}
\input{results/table4_baseline.tex}
```

Baseline: agreement with the reference HMC, block group constraint leaf cells of
the four PUMAs pooled. Median diff.: $|$median $-$ reference median$|$ in reference
standard deviations; width ratio: the 90 percent interval's width over the
reference's; p50, p99 and p10 are percentiles over cells. k-hat: the PSIS $\hat k$
of the method's density against the posterior, one per fit, median [min, max] over
PUMAs (methods with a density only).

:::

::: {#tbl-agree-tract}

```{=latex}
\input{results/table4t_baseline.tex}
```

Baseline: agreement with the reference HMC for tract constraint leaf cells. As
@tbl-agree; $\hat k$, one per fit, is in @tbl-agree.

:::

@tbl-agree compares each approximation with the reference posterior cell by cell,
in units of the reference standard deviation. The short HMC run is
indistinguishable from the reference in its medians (median difference 0.01 sd;
99th percentile 0.06) and in the typical width of its intervals (median ratio 0.99
to 1.00). At $\alpha = 0.01$, however, a tenth of cells have intervals no more than
a third as wide as the reference's (10th percentile ratio 0.34, against 0.92 at
$\alpha = 1$); the short run explores some directions of the more weakly
identified $\alpha = 0.01$ posterior incompletely. The variational fits match the
reference's typical interval widths (median ratio 0.92 to 1.05) but not its tails.
At $\alpha = 0.01$, some cells' medians are off by nearly one reference sd (99th
percentile 0.88 to 0.95), and a tenth of cells have intervals less than five
percent as wide as the reference's. The PSIS $\hat{k}$ diagnostic, which compares
each variational density with the posterior jointly rather than cell by cell, is
far above the threshold of 0.7 for every variational fit (11 to 23 in the
baseline) [@vehtari2024pareto]; although their marginal summaries are close to the
reference, their joint distributions are not. The Laplace approximation fails on
every measure. IPF's solution is [UPDATE] reference sd from the reference medians
at the 50th percentile, against 0.14 to 0.17 for the variational fits at
$\alpha = 0.01$, and [UPDATE] at the 99th.

### Usability of the draws {#sec-supp-usable}

::: {.landscape}

::: {#tbl-usable}

```{=latex}
\input{results/table5_baseline.tex}
```

Baseline: usability of the draws. Draws of the four PUMAs pooled (4,000 per PUMA;
IPF's one fit per PUMA, shown as counts of its four fits). A cell is one survey
record in one block group. Draws with a cell $> 0.01\,N$: the share of draws in
which one cell holds more than one percent of the PUMA's households. D/H: a block
group's expected number of distinct records among its $H$ published households,
drawn by the records' shares, per household (@sec-measures-usability); for each
draw its smallest over the block groups with more than 100 published households.
$n_{\mathrm{eff}} = 1/\sum s^2$ over the same shares. Households $|z|$: a block
group's allocated occupied households against B25003, with the SE from its cells'
variances; for each draw its largest over block groups.

:::

:::

@tbl-usable asks whether individual draws are plausible populations. The Laplace
draws are not. In every draw a single survey record accounts for more than one
percent of a PUMA's households, the least diverse block group has a D/H near zero
(median 0.001 at $\alpha = 0.01$ and 0.002 at $\alpha = 1$) and an effective
number of records of one, and the largest departure of a block group's household
count from its published value is hundreds of standard errors.

Variational draws are much better but often still implausible. At
$\alpha = 0.01$, about four in five variational Gaussian draws contain a record
holding more than one percent of the PUMA's households (80 percent; 77 percent for
the skewed family), and [UPDATE] percent have a block group with D/H below 0.04, a
value no reference draw reaches. Their typical draw is nonetheless close to the
reference's: the median of the smallest D/H is 0.099 for the variational Gaussian
and 0.108 for the reference at $\alpha = 0.01$, and 0.259 and 0.284 at
$\alpha = 1$. The failures are therefore in the tails of the variational
distribution, rare enough to leave the small area summaries of @sec-supp-fit
largely unaffected but each of them an implausible population. No HMC draw
contains a dominant record, and no reference draw has a block group below the D/H
floor.

The HMC results also show that concentrated draws are partly a property of the
posterior itself, not only of the approximation. At $\alpha = 0.01$, 80 percent of
reference draws have at least one block group with fewer than ten effective
records, and the median of the smallest effective number of records is 6.6; at
$\alpha = 1$, the share falls to 13 percent and the median rises to 21. The weakly
identified directions of the correlated covariance allow even exact posterior draws
to concentrate a block group's households on fewer records. IPF's multinomial
replicates [UPDATE: their share under ten effective records and their smallest
D/H]. For population synthesis, the choice of covariance therefore matters as much
as the choice of algorithm.

[AUTHOR: In about half ($\alpha = 0.01$) to four-fifths ($\alpha = 1$) of HMC draws,
at least one block group's allocated households lie more than five standard errors
from the published count (median of the largest $|z|$ 4.95 and 6.52). Because this
is a maximum over several hundred block groups, some large values are expected even
for a correct model, but not values this large. Explanation needed before
publication.]

### Computation time {#sec-supp-cost}

::: {#tbl-cost}

```{=latex}
\input{results/table1_baseline.tex}
```

Baseline: minutes per PUMA, mean over the four PUMAs. Fit: raking, MAP, or MAP and
the variational fit; for HMC, the variational Gaussian fit that whitens it.
Sampling: Laplace and drawing, variational drawing (with rejection when truncated),
or HMC. Fits ran on 48-core CPU nodes, HMC on one GPU.

:::

@tbl-cost reports computation time per PUMA. MAP with the Laplace approximation
takes about a minute. The variational fits take about one to two hours (48 to 129
minutes), almost all of it fitting; once fitted, their draws cost almost nothing.
The short HMC run adds 10 to 27 minutes of sampling to the variational fit that
whitens it, while the reference run adds 5 to 16 hours. Every posterior method is
faster at $\alpha = 1$ than at $\alpha = 0.01$ (reference HMC: 329 against 1,033
minutes), consistent with the poorer conditioning of the nearly singular replicate
covariance. IPF takes [UPDATE] minutes.

## Effect of the remedies {#sec-supp-remedies}

*Null space* (@sec-supp-null). Removing all structural dependencies changes small
area accuracy and agreement with the reference little. The main differences are at
$\alpha = 1$. Fitted block group cells are matched more closely (variational
Gaussian $|z|$ p90 0.87 against 1.16), and fewer HMC draws have a household count
more than five standard errors off (59 against 80 percent). The costs are somewhat
more concentrated draws (median smallest effective number of records 14.8 against
21.0) and longer runs (reference HMC 532 against 329 minutes).

*Roll-up* (@sec-supp-rollup). Merging small cells has the largest practical effect.
It shortens every variational and HMC computation by a factor of three to six
(reference HMC 309 against 1,033 minutes at $\alpha = 0.01$; variational Gaussian 14
against 70), and it makes variational draws much more usable: at $\alpha = 1$, the
share of draws with a dominant record falls from 38 to 9 percent, and the share
with a block group under ten effective records from 76 to 44 percent. Roll-up also
rescues the Laplace approximation for small area estimation at $\alpha = 1$, whose
intervals now match the published margins of error (ratio 0.98) and contain the
published value in 83 percent of fitted cells, although 95 percent of its draws
still contain a dominant record. The cost is a small loss of accuracy on held-out
tables at $\alpha = 1$ (coverage [UPDATE] against [UPDATE]). Because
roll-up changes the set of constraint cells, its fitted-cell and agreement results
are not directly comparable with the other experiments'; its held-out results are.
